Takeuchi information criterion

TIC.Rd

Computes the Takeuchi information criterion (TIC), a version of AIC whose penalty remains valid if the model is misspecified, for one or several fitted models.

Usage

TIC(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'LaMaModel'
TIC(
  object,
  ...,
  type = c("HAC", "sandwich", "cluster"),
  kernel = c("QS", "Bartlett"),
  bw = NULL,
  cluster = NULL,
  cr = c("CR1", "CR0", "CR3")
)

Arguments

object

model object of class "LaMaModel"

...

further models of class "LaMaModel", compared as in AIC

type

robust covariance used for the penalty: "HAC" (default), "sandwich" or "cluster", see vcov.LaMaModel

kernel, bw, cluster, cr

passed to vcov.LaMaModel

Value

For one model, the TIC, with the effective number of parameters as attribute "edf". For several, a data frame with one row per model and columns df (number of parameters), edf and TIC.

Details

With \(H\) the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood and \(J\) the variance of the score sum (the meat of the sandwich, see vcov.LaMaModel), $$\mathrm{TIC} = -2 \log L(\hat\theta) + 2 \, \mathrm{edf}, \qquad \mathrm{edf} = \mathrm{tr}(J H^{-1}).$$ The penalty of AIC, the number of parameters \(p\), assumes \(J = H\), which holds if the model is correctly specified. TIC estimates it instead: the effective number of parameters edf approximates the optimism \(E[(\hat\theta - \theta^*)^\top H (\hat\theta - \theta^*)] \approx \mathrm{tr}(H \, \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta))\) of the maximised log-likelihood, so models whose estimates are more variable than the model itself suggests are penalised more.

It is computed from the robust covariance \(V = H^{-1} J H^{-1}\) as \(\mathrm{edf} = \mathrm{tr}(H V)\), so every robust type of vcov.LaMaModel can be used, including the jackknife cr = "CR3". The default is the HAC sandwich, as the penalty needs the correct variance of the estimator, which for serially dependent scores is not given by the outer product of the scores (type = "sandwich"). For several independent tracks, type = "cluster" is an alternative.

Under correct specification, edf is close to \(p\), and TIC close to AIC. Values well above \(p\) indicate misspecification, e.g. serial dependence the model misses. Values below \(p\) arise from noise in the estimated \(J\), from a model that overstates the variability of the data, or from parameters that are nearly not identified, e.g. a superfluous state. In the last case, neither AIC nor TIC is justified, so neither should be used to choose the number of states. edf is itself estimated and, especially for short series, noisy.

References

Takeuchi, K. (1976). Distribution of informational statistics and a criterion of model fitting. Suri-Kagaku (Mathematical Sciences), 153, 12–18 (in Japanese).

Konishi, S. and Kitagawa, G. (2008). Information Criteria and Statistical Modeling. Springer, New York.
